claim: Mouse primary somatosensory barrel cortex (wS1) processes whisker sensory information.
source: Mouse primary somatosensory barrel cortex (wS1) processes whisker sensory information, receiving input from two distinct thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: wS1 receives input from two distinct thalamic nuclei.
source: Mouse primary somatosensory barrel cortex (wS1) processes whisker sensory information, receiving input from two distinct thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ventral posterior medial (VPM) somatosensory thalamic nucleus is a first-order nucleus.
source: The first-order ventral posterior medial (VPM) somatosensory thalamic nucleus most densely innervates layer 4 (L4) barrels
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: VPM most densely innervates layer 4 (L4) barrels in wS1.
source: The first-order ventral posterior medial (VPM) somatosensory thalamic nucleus most densely innervates layer 4 (L4) barrels
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The posterior thalamic nucleus (medial part, POm) is a higher-order nucleus.
source: whereas the higher-order posterior thalamic nucleus (medial part, POm) most densely innervates L1 and L5A.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: POm most densely innervates L1 and L5A in wS1.
source: whereas the higher-order posterior thalamic nucleus (medial part, POm) most densely innervates L1 and L5A.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Excitatory neurons received the largest EPSPs from thalamic input.
source: We found that excitatory neurons and parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons received the largest EPSPs, dominated by VPM input to L4 and POm input to L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-8 and Tables 1-4.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons received the largest EPSPs from thalamic input.
source: We found that excitatory neurons and parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons received the largest EPSPs, dominated by VPM input to L4 and POm input to L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4-5 and Tables 1-4.

claim: VPM input to L4 dominates the thalamic input to excitatory and PV neurons.
source: We found that excitatory neurons and parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons received the largest EPSPs, dominated by VPM input to L4 and POm input to L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 4, 8 and Tables 1-2.

claim: POm input to L5A dominates the thalamic input to excitatory and PV neurons.
source: We found that excitatory neurons and parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons received the largest EPSPs, dominated by VPM input to L4 and POm input to L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 5, 8 and Tables 3-4.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons received very little input from either VPM or POm in any layer.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons received very little input from either pathway in any layer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Tables 1-4.

claim: Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing inhibitory neurons received an intermediate level of excitatory input.
source: Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing inhibitory neurons received an intermediate level of excitatory input with less apparent layer-specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Tables 1-4.

claim: VIP neurons received thalamic input with less apparent layer-specificity compared to other cell types.
source: Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing inhibitory neurons received an intermediate level of excitatory input with less apparent layer-specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Tables 1-4.

claim: All cortical areas receive thalamic input.
source: All cortical areas receive thalamic input, with different thalamic nuclei projecting to different cortical regions and layers (Clascá et al., 2012; Herkenham, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different thalamic nuclei project to different cortical regions and layers.
source: All cortical areas receive thalamic input, with different thalamic nuclei projecting to different cortical regions and layers (Clascá et al., 2012; Herkenham, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The lateral geniculate nucleus innervates primary visual cortex.
source: Primary sensory cortical areas receive thalamic input from primary sensory thalamic nuclei - for example the lateral geniculate nucleus innervates primary visual cortex, the medial geniculate nucleus innervates primary auditory cortex and the lateral and medial portions of the ventral posterior nucleus innervate primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The medial geniculate nucleus innervates primary auditory cortex.
source: Primary sensory cortical areas receive thalamic input from primary sensory thalamic nuclei - for example the lateral geniculate nucleus innervates primary visual cortex, the medial geniculate nucleus innervates primary auditory cortex and the lateral and medial portions of the ventral posterior nucleus innervate primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The lateral and medial portions of the ventral posterior nucleus innervate primary somatosensory cortex.
source: Primary sensory cortical areas receive thalamic input from primary sensory thalamic nuclei - for example the lateral geniculate nucleus innervates primary visual cortex, the medial geniculate nucleus innervates primary auditory cortex and the lateral and medial portions of the ventral posterior nucleus innervate primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Primary sensory thalamic input to primary sensory areas is arranged in topographic maps.
source: The primary sensory thalamic input to primary sensory areas is arranged in topographic maps, for example retinotopy in visual cortex, tonotopy in auditory cortex, and somatotopy in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Innervation from primary sensory thalamus is densest in layer 4 (L4) of the neocortex.
source: Anatomically, the innervation from primary sensory thalamus is densest in layer 4 (L4) of the neocortex, but also present in all other cortical layers (Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Primary sensory thalamic innervation is present in all cortical layers.
source: Anatomically, the innervation from primary sensory thalamus is densest in layer 4 (L4) of the neocortex, but also present in all other cortical layers (Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Primary sensory thalamic input is thought to drive sensory processing in the recipient cortex.
source: The primary sensory thalamic input is thought to drive sensory processing in the recipient cortex (Reinhold et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice receive important tactile sensory information from their array of mystacial whiskers.
source: Mice receive important tactile sensory information about their immediate surroundings from their array of mystacial whiskers (Diamond et al., 2008; Feldmeyer et al., 2013; Petersen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The whisker representation in mouse primary somatosensory cortex (wS1) is arranged in discrete anatomical units termed 'barrels'.
source: The whisker representation in mouse primary somatosensory cortex (wS1) is arranged in discrete anatomical units, termed 'barrels', with each barrel representing an individual whisker on the snout (Woolsey and Van der Loos, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Each barrel represents an individual whisker on the snout.
source: The whisker representation in mouse primary somatosensory cortex (wS1) is arranged in discrete anatomical units, termed 'barrels', with each barrel representing an individual whisker on the snout (Woolsey and Van der Loos, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Barrels are found in L4 of wS1.
source: The barrels are found in L4 of wS1, and each barrel is densely innervated by neurons located in the homologous 'barreloid' of the ventral posterior medial (VPM) primary whisker somatosensory thalamus (Arnold et al., 2001; Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each barrel is densely innervated by neurons located in the homologous 'barreloid' of VPM.
source: The barrels are found in L4 of wS1, and each barrel is densely innervated by neurons located in the homologous 'barreloid' of the ventral posterior medial (VPM) primary whisker somatosensory thalamus (Arnold et al., 2001; Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VPM axons are densest in L4.
source: Although VPM axons are densest in L4, there is also substantial VPM axon innervation of L3 above the barrels and at the border of L5 and L6 (Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and anatomical data in Figure 1A.

claim: There is substantial VPM axon innervation of L3 above the barrels and at the border of L5 and L6.
source: Although VPM axons are densest in L4, there is also substantial VPM axon innervation of L3 above the barrels and at the border of L5 and L6 (Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and anatomical data in Figure 1A.

claim: Dendritic arborizations of postsynaptic neurons in wS1 span different cortical layers.
source: In many cases, the dendritic arborizations of postsynaptic neurons in wS1 span different cortical layers and therefore neurons with cell-bodies located in many different, if not all, layers could receive synaptic input from VPM (Meyer et al., 2010; Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons with cell-bodies located in many different layers could receive synaptic input from VPM.
source: In many cases, the dendritic arborizations of postsynaptic neurons in wS1 span different cortical layers and therefore neurons with cell-bodies located in many different, if not all, layers could receive synaptic input from VPM (Meyer et al., 2010; Oberlaender et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and inference from dendritic spanning.

claim: Stimulation of VPM axons evokes excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in various cortical layers.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, previous electrophysiological studies have found that stimulation of VPM axons evokes excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in various cortical layers (Bureau et al., 2006; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Largely non-overlapping populations of inhibitory GABAergic neurons are classified through expression of parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
source: There are many different types of neocortical neurons, with largely non-overlapping populations of inhibitory GABAergic neurons being classified through expression of parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Feldmeyer et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2010; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VPM provides the largest synaptic input to PV neurons.
source: Previous work has found that VPM provides the largest synaptic input to PV neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2007), and substantially less to SST neurons, but systematic quantification of VPM input to different cell-types across layers in a single study is currently lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: VPM provides substantially less synaptic input to SST neurons compared to PV neurons.
source: Previous work has found that VPM provides the largest synaptic input to PV neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2007), and substantially less to SST neurons, but systematic quantification of VPM input to different cell-types across layers in a single study is currently lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Systematic quantification of VPM input to different cell-types across layers in a single study is currently lacking.
source: Previous work has found that VPM provides the largest synaptic input to PV neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2007), and substantially less to SST neurons, but systematic quantification of VPM input to different cell-types across layers in a single study is currently lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: POm is considered a higher-order thalamic area.
source: POm is considered a higher-order thalamic area, since it receives strong 'driver' input from excitatory L5B neurons in wS1 (Groh et al., 2008; Mease et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: POm receives strong 'driver' input from excitatory L5B neurons in wS1.
source: POm is considered a higher-order thalamic area, since it receives strong 'driver' input from excitatory L5B neurons in wS1 (Groh et al., 2008; Mease et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inactivation of wS1 potently inhibits both spontaneous and whisker deflection-evoked action potential firing of many POm neurons.
source: and inactivation of wS1 potently inhibits both spontaneous and whisker deflection-evoked action potential firing of many POm neurons (Diamond et al., 1992; Mease et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: POm axons densely innervate L1 and L5A in wS1, forming a complementary pattern to the VPM innervation.
source: POm axons densely innervate L1 and L5A in wS1, forming a complementary pattern to the VPM innervation (Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and anatomical data in Figure 1A.

claim: Stimulation of POm axons evokes EPSPs in excitatory neurons with cell bodies in various layers, with strong responses found in L5A.
source: Stimulation of POm axons evokes EPSPs in excitatory neurons with cell bodies in various layers, with strong responses found in L5A (Audette et al., 2018; Bureau et al., 2006; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Large responses to POm stimulation were found in PV neurons.
source: Large responses to POm stimulation were also found in PV neurons (Audette et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: GPR26-Cre mice specifically express Cre-recombinase in higher-order thalamus (including POm) but not first-order thalamus (i.e. VPM).
source: In some experiments (n = 12 mice), we used GPR26-Cre mice, which specifically express Cre-recombinase in higher-order thalamus (including POm) but not first-order thalamus (i.e. VPM) (Gerfen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Injection of virus encoding Cre-ON sequences (FLEX/DIO) into GPR26-Cre mice induced expression in POm, but not VPM.
source: Injection of virus encoding Cre-ON sequences (FLEX/DIO) into these mice, induced expression in POm, but not VPM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Injection of virus encoding a Cre-OFF element (DFO) into GPR26-Cre mice induced expression in VPM, but not POm.
source: Conversely, injection of virus encoding a Cre-OFF element (DFO) (Fenno et al., 2014) induced expression in VPM, but not POm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to prior literature.

claim: In mice, VPM strongly innervated L4 barrels in wS1, as well as innervating L3 above the barrels and the border of L5 and L6.
source: Consistent with previously published anatomy in rats (Meyer et al., 2010; Wimmer et al., 2010), we found that in mice VPM strongly innervated L4 barrels in wS1, as well as innervating L3 above the barrels and the border of L5 and L6
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior literature.

claim: In mice, POm strongly innervated L5A and L1 in wS1.
source: whereas POm strongly innervated L5A and L1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Blue light flashes evoked monosynaptic EPSPs in wS1 neurons under the experimental conditions used.
source: Under these experimental conditions, we found that blue light flashes evoked monosynaptic EPSPs in wS1 neurons, which were completely blocked by application of CNQX (20 µM) and APV (50 µM) to block AMPA and NMDA ionotropic glutamate receptors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Optogenetically-evoked EPSPs were completely blocked by application of CNQX and APV.
source: Under these experimental conditions, we found that blue light flashes evoked monosynaptic EPSPs in wS1 neurons, which were completely blocked by application of CNQX (20 µM) and APV (50 µM) to block AMPA and NMDA ionotropic glutamate receptors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On average there was no change in the amplitude of evoked EPSPs comparing those recorded in the first minutes of the whole-cell recording to those measured more than an hour later in the same cells.
source: We found that on average there was no change in the amplitude of evoked EPSPs comparing those recorded in the first minutes of the whole-cell recording to those measured more than an hour later in the same cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L2 excitatory neurons was 2.0 ± 5.3 mV (n = 29 cells).
source: The mean peak amplitude of EPSPs according to the laminar location of the cell somata was: L2, 2.0 ± 5.3 mV (n = 29 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L3 excitatory neurons was 6.7 ± 7.2 mV (n = 45 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L4 excitatory neurons was 14.5 ± 7.4 mV (n = 65 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L5A excitatory neurons was 1.7 ± 2.1 mV (n = 39 cells).
source: L5A, 1.7 ± 2.1 mV (n = 39 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L5B excitatory neurons was 2.3 ± 2.9 mV (n = 44 cells).
source: L5B, 2.3 ± 2.9 mV (n = 44 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of VPM-evoked EPSPs in L6 excitatory neurons was 3.5 ± 6.7 mV (n = 40 cells).
source: and L6, 3.5 ± 6.7 mV (n = 40 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Excitatory neurons across all cortical layers receive input from VPM.
source: Excitatory neurons across all cortical layers therefore receive input from VPM, and in each layer some neurons receive much stronger input than the average.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In each layer some excitatory neurons receive much stronger VPM input than the average.
source: Excitatory neurons across all cortical layers therefore receive input from VPM, and in each layer some neurons receive much stronger input than the average.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The amplitude and slope of both normalized and absolute VPM-evoked EPSPs in L4 excitatory neurons were significantly larger than the input to any other layer.
source: The amplitude and slope of both normalized and absolute EPSPs in L4 were significantly larger than the input to any other layer (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<10−7 for each comparison).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L2 excitatory neurons was 1.3 ± 2.6 mV (n = 38 cells).
source: The mean peak amplitude of EPSPs for each layer was: L2, 1.3 ± 2.6 mV (n = 38 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L3 excitatory neurons was 1.8 ± 4.0 mV (n = 31 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L4 excitatory neurons was 1.3 ± 3.5 mV (n = 38 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L5A excitatory neurons was 11.7 ± 7.8 mV (n = 75 cells).
source: L5A, 11.7 ± 7.8 mV (n = 75 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L5B excitatory neurons was 1.4 ± 4.6 mV (n = 52 cells).
source: L5B, 1.4 ± 4.6 mV (n = 52 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of POm-evoked EPSPs in L6 excitatory neurons was 1.6 ± 2.4 mV (n = 47 cells).
source: and L6, 1.6 ± 2.4 mV (n = 47 cells)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both slope and amplitude of the normalized and absolute POm-evoked EPSPs were significantly larger in L5A compared to any other layer.
source: Both slope and amplitude of the normalized and absolute EPSPs were significantly larger in L5A compared to any other layer (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<10−7 for each comparison).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: VPM input to PV neurons in L4 was about three times stronger than the input onto PV neurons in L3 for both EPSP amplitude and slope.
source: VPM input to PV neurons in L4 was found to be about three times stronger than the input onto PV neurons in L3 for both EPSP amplitude and slope.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Tables 1-2.

claim: The overall laminar pattern of VPM input is similar for PV neurons and excitatory neurons.
source: The overall laminar pattern of VPM input is therefore similar for PV neurons and excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 4, and 8.

claim: The EPSP peak amplitudes for PV neurons are comparable to the excitatory neurons for each layer.
source: The EPSP peak amplitudes for PV neurons are also comparable to the excitatory neurons for each layer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 4, and 8.

claim: The EPSP slope is larger in PV neurons compared to excitatory neurons.
source: However, the EPSP slope is larger in PV neurons compared to excitatory neurons, with the L4 PV neurons having an almost three times larger EPSP slope compared to L4 excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 4, and 8.

claim: L4 PV neurons have an almost three times larger EPSP slope compared to L4 excitatory neurons in response to VPM stimulation.
source: However, the EPSP slope is larger in PV neurons compared to excitatory neurons, with the L4 PV neurons having an almost three times larger EPSP slope compared to L4 excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 4, and 8.

claim: The VPM input to L4 PV neurons was significantly larger than input to PV neurons in other layers for both amplitude and slope.
source: Comparing across layers, the VPM input to L4 PV neurons was significantly larger than input to PV neurons in other layers for both amplitude and slope (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05 for each comparison).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The laminar distribution of POm input to PV neurons is similar to that of excitatory neurons.
source: The laminar distribution of POm input to PV neurons is similar to that of excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 5, and 8.

claim: The EPSP amplitude in L5A is similar in PV and excitatory neurons in response to POm stimulation.
source: Whereas the EPSP amplitude in L5A is similar in PV and excitatory neurons, the slope of the EPSP in L5A PV neurons is twice as large as that of the L5A excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 5, and 8.

claim: The slope of the EPSP in L5A PV neurons is twice as large as that of the L5A excitatory neurons in response to POm stimulation.
source: Whereas the EPSP amplitude in L5A is similar in PV and excitatory neurons, the slope of the EPSP in L5A PV neurons is twice as large as that of the L5A excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 5, and 8.

claim: The POm input to L5A PV neurons was significantly larger than input to PV neurons in other layers for both amplitude and slope.
source: Comparing across layers, the POm input to L5A PV neurons was significantly larger than input to PV neurons in other layers for both amplitude and slope (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05 for each comparison).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The VPM-evoked peak EPSP amplitudes and EPSP slopes in SST neurons across all layers were small compared to the L4 excitatory neurons within the same slice.
source: The VPM-evoked peak EPSP amplitudes and EPSP slopes in SST neurons across all layers were small compared to the L4 excitatory neurons within the same slice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Tables 1-2.

claim: The largest mean VPM-evoked EPSP amplitudes in SST neurons were found in L3 and L4, but even these were approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the mean input to the excitatory neurons.
source: The largest mean EPSP amplitudes in SST neurons were found in L3 and L4, but even these were approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the mean input to the excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Tables 1-2.

claim: POm input to SST neurons was largest in L5A, but this was nonetheless more than five times smaller than the POm input to excitatory neurons in L5A.
source: The POm input to SST neurons was largest in L5A, but this was nonetheless more than five times smaller than the POm input to excitatory neurons in L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Tables 3-4.

claim: SST neurons receive facilitating excitatory input both in vitro and in vivo.
source: A robust characteristic of SST neurons is that they receive facilitating excitatory input both in vitro (Kapfer et al., 2007; Reyes et al., 1998; Silberberg and Markram, 2007) and in vivo (Pala and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Facilitation was absent in SST neurons under the recording conditions used in this study.
source: However, we found that facilitation was absent in SST neurons under our recording conditions, presumably because optogenetic stimulation evokes large calcium spikes in the presence of TTX and 4-AP driving neurotransmitter release with high probability.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Most VIP neurons received relatively little thalamic input.
source: Most VIP neurons received relatively little thalamic input, but in each layer we found some strongly innervated VIP neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In each layer some VIP neurons were strongly innervated by thalamic input.
source: Most VIP neurons received relatively little thalamic input, but in each layer we found some strongly innervated VIP neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: VIP neurons on average appear to receive thalamic input with less dependence upon the location of the cell body compared to excitatory and PV neurons.
source: In contrast to excitatory and PV neurons, the VIP neurons on average appear to receive thalamic input with less dependence upon the location of the cell body.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Tables 1-4.

claim: VIP neurons in L3 received the largest VPM input, which was roughly twice as large as the EPSP amplitude in L2, L4 and L5B.
source: VIP neurons in L3 received the largest VPM input, which was roughly twice as large as the EPSP amplitude in L2, L4 and L5B.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Tables 1-2.

claim: POm input to VIP neurons appeared to be distributed more-or-less evenly across layers, with a somewhat larger mean EPSP in L5A.
source: POm input to VIP neurons appeared to be distributed more-or-less evenly across layers, with a somewhat larger mean EPSP in L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Tables 3-4.

claim: VPM and POm input to excitatory and PV neurons is much stronger than the thalamic input to SST neurons.
source: Our data suggest that VPM and POm input to excitatory and PV neurons is much stronger than the thalamic input to SST neurons, with VIP neurons receiving an intermediate level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-8 and Tables 1-4.

claim: VIP neurons receive an intermediate level of thalamic input compared to excitatory/PV neurons and SST neurons.
source: Our data suggest that VPM and POm input to excitatory and PV neurons is much stronger than the thalamic input to SST neurons, with VIP neurons receiving an intermediate level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-8 and Tables 1-4.

claim: Input to excitatory, PV and SST neurons largely appears to follow the pattern of axonal innervation density.
source: Input to excitatory, PV and SST neurons largely appears to follow the pattern of axonal innervation density, with VPM most strongly innervating L4 (and L3), and POm most strongly innervating L5A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-8.

claim: VIP neurons appear to receive thalamic input with less layer-dependence compared to other cell types.
source: VIP neurons appear to receive thalamic input with less layer-dependence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Tables 1-4.

claim: VPM input is thought to dominate the earliest wS1 sensory responses evoked by whisker deflection.
source: Thalamic input from VPM is thought to dominate the earliest wS1 sensory responses evoked by whisker deflection (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Cohen-Kashi Malina et al., 2016; Gutnisky et al., 2017; Oberlaender et al., 2012a; Pinto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in L4 of wS1 on average depolarize in response to whisker deflection with shorter latencies and larger amplitudes than neurons in other layers.
source: Neurons in L4 of wS1 on average depolarize in response to whisker deflection with shorter latencies and larger amplitudes than neurons in other layers (Brecht et al., 2003; Brecht and Sakmann, 2002; Manns et al., 2004; Moore and Nelson, 1998; Zhu and Connors, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During active touch, neurons in deeper parts of L2/3 on average depolarize more rapidly and strongly than neurons in superficial L2/3.
source: During active touch, neurons in deeper parts of L2/3 on average depolarize more rapidly and strongly than neurons in superficial L2/3 (Crochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A brief whisker deflection evokes action potential firing with shortest latency in L4 and L5B.
source: A brief whisker deflection evokes action potential firing with shortest latency in L4 and L5B (Armstrong-James et al., 1992; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; de Kock et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During texture sampling, action potentials in L4 are evoked at the shortest latencies in response to whisker slips.
source: During texture sampling, whiskers exhibit rapid slips as they overcome surface friction, and these slips evoke rapid sensory responses in wS1, with action potentials in L4 being evoked at the shortest latencies (Isett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.
